name: Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
overview: In the heart of Yaoundé, Efoulan describes itself as a “mixture of peoples”: the Ewondo live there with Basaa, people from the Grassfields and from the North. Like all the Beti, they say they crossed the Sanaga on the back of a mythical snake. Catholic and highly urbanised, they keep the olugu, respect for elders, and the music of the balafon and the tam-tam.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group but integrated into a very mixed environment (Basaa, Grassfields, peoples of the North).
Ewondo is spoken in the Centre, South and East.
Marriage within the group is forbidden: alliances are formed with other groups.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land, with no religious value: it was Charles Atangana Ntsama who brought the missionaries there.
Like the Beti as a whole, the group crossed the Sanaga on the mythical serpent and first settled at Ngwa Ekələ, on the Atəməŋgə plateau; ties with these places remain.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship, age and kinship organise society; the family deliberates and then approaches the chief, who convenes and decides by consensus.
Among the Beti, an unmarried man does not speak in public and was not entitled to the essani at his death.
A man's inheritance stays in his family.
The olugu, respect for elders, family and blood ties, governs life together.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship today; the wife joins her husband's family.
No one declares a boy a man or a girl a woman: each person asserts it for themselves.
Steps: ekud mbɛ́ (“knocking at the door”, because the boy formerly entered by the window), then nsi lí alug, the marriage proposal where the bride price list is handed over.
Bride price: red wine, a big goat (ekut kabet) for the girl's parents, aŋgámbá wán.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The group is Catholic and no longer has an ancestor cult.
Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator.
Taboos: incest, contempt for elders.
Transgressions led to quarantine (mimbok mi dzal); incest required an expiatory rite with a goat or a sheep.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men and women: trade (mákit), pig and poultry rearing.
The land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching agreement with the neighbours in order to draw up the papers.
Basketry, pottery and sculpture, practised by the ancestors, have disappeared.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Traditional dress is no longer followed: everyone dresses as they wish.
Traditional medicine remains effective and widely used.
Beauty is considered relative and personal.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Music: miŋkúl (tam-tam) and məjaŋ (balafon).
Dances: asiko ŋnam, osilaa, ɲəʒ.
The former community festivals have disappeared.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The chiefdom has been passed down since Charles Atangana Ntsama.
Like the other groups of central Yaoundé, Efoulan is strongly marked by Western influence and by migration.

sections.title: The names
items: Everyone names their child as they wish; only the name ŋdəŋhə is reserved for men.
One does not change name; a pseudonym is sometimes used.
The founding ancestor is called Ataŋgana Esomba.

lessons.title: Who are the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group but integrated into a very mixed environment (Basaa, Grassfields, peoples of the North). • Ewondo is spoken in the Centre, the South and the East. • Marriage within the group is forbidden: alliances are made with other groups. • Ancestral land, with no religious value: it was Charles Atangana Ntsama who brought the missionaries there. • Like the Beti as a whole, the group crossed the Sanaga on the mythical serpent and first settled at Ngwa Ekələ, on the Atəməŋgə plateau; ties with these places remain.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the heart of Yaoundé, Efoulan describes itself as a “mixture of peoples”: the Ewondo live there with Basaa, people from the Grassfields and from the North. Like all the Beti, they say they crossed the Sanaga on the back of a mythical snake. Catholic and highly urbanised, they keep the olugu, respect for elders, and the music of the balafon and the tam-tam.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kpəm (cassava leaves). • Drinks: palm wine (məjɔg malen). • Men and women: trade (mákit), rearing pigs and poultry.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) mainly eat kpəm. Traditional drinks: məjɔg malen. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), traditional dances (asiko ŋnam, osilaa, ɲəʒ) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: ŋkúl tam-tam, məjaŋ balafon.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men and women: trade (mákit), rearing of pigs and poultry. • Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching an agreement with the neighbours to draw up the papers. • Basketry, pottery and sculpture, practised by the ancestors, have disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men and women: trade (mákit), pig and poultry rearing. Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching an agreement with the neighbours to draw up the papers.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I propose

student.memo: Men and women: trade (mákit), pig and poultry rearing. Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought by reaching an agreement with the neighbours to draw up the papers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The group is Catholic and no longer has ancestor worship. • Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator. • Taboos: incest, contempt for elders. • Transgressions led to quarantine (mimbok mi dzal); incest required an expiatory rite with a goat or a sheep.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The group is Catholic and no longer has ancestor worship. Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I compare

student.memo: The group is Catholic and no longer has ancestor worship. Birth is the joy of the family; death, the return to the Creator.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ewondo
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Ewondo. • Greeting formulas: Masuk = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Mbembə kiri = morning greeting (one person); Mini vuman = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔg, Bɛ, Lɛ, ɲi, tan. • The founding ancestor is called Ataŋgana Esomba. • The chiefdom has been passed on since Charles Atangana Ntsama.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ewondo are the first steps towards communicating with the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Ewondo.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Ewondo are the first steps towards communicating with the Ewondo (Mvog Tsung, Mbala). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
